top.title: Vitamin C could help block cancer-linked chemicals in your stomach, study finds
top.summary: Scientists have discovered that vitamin C may help prevent potentially cancer-causing chemicals from forming in the stomach after eating foods containing nitrates and nitrites. A new mathematical model suggests that taking vitamin C after meals could reduce these harmful reactions, offering a possible new strategy for lowering cancer risk.

more.title: New observations challenge evidence for an 'outsize' black hole in the early universe
more.summary: A recent reanalysis of the outsize black hole galaxy UHZ1 using existing X-ray data and new infrared observations challenges a previous groundbreaking claim. Three years ago, this galaxy made news for hosting an unusually massive and heavily dust-obscured black hole formed through direct collapse. Led by Fan Zou of the University of Michigan, the new study reports no signs of hidden black hole activity.

more.title: A common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in a surprising new study
more.summary: Scientists have uncovered a surprising genetic connection to spinal degeneration and found that an existing osteoporosis drug can prevent damaging mineral buildup in zebrafish spines. The discovery could pave the way for new treatments that slow or prevent a major cause of chronic back pain.

more.title: Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses
more.summary: Scientists have discovered a strange stellar pair more than 5,000 light-years away, where a dead star spinning every eight minutes produces mysterious radio pulses while orbiting a Sun-like star. The breakthrough also revealed massive magnetic storms on the companion star, offering fresh clues to one of astronomy's emerging mysteries.

more.title: A simple supplement could help your immune system fight cancer and viral infections
more.summary: A surprising discovery from Rockefeller University suggests that a common amino acid could play a powerful role in protecting against cancer and viral infections. Scientists found that low arginine levels interfere with the immune system's ability to recognize dangerous cells, while increasing arginine intake reduced colon cancer tumors and improved viral infection outcomes in mice.

more.title: Why aging stars suffer a sudden luminosity dip
more.summary: From a naked-eye perspective, stars are stable and predictable. Not much goes on but shining. The sun itself is fairly plain and nondescript and will shine relatively steadily for billions of years. It's considered a low-mass star compared to the most massive stars, which are rarer and contain many times its mass.

more.title: Milk and wine used in Menorcan funerary rituals over 2,000 years ago
more.summary: In the Late Iron Age, or post-Talayotic period, over 2,000 years ago, Menorca and the other Balearic Islands experienced increasing connectivity with the wider Mediterranean. However, they also maintained distinctive local funerary traditions, such as burying their loved ones in rock-cut tombs, or artificial caves.

more.title: Archaeologists uncover a witness to the Neolithic revolution
more.summary: Radiocarbon dating and isotope analysis of an immaculately preserved skeleton from Mesolithic Denmark indicate that the individual lived through the introduction of agriculture and adapted his diet to the change, providing a unique "eyewitness account" of one of humanity's most significant technological revolutions.

more.title: Uranus and Neptune’s bizarre magnetic fields may finally be explained
more.summary: The strange, wildly tilted magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune have puzzled scientists since NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft explored the planets in the 1980s. New simulations suggest that extreme conditions deep inside these icy giants create unusual electrical properties that could explain their magnetic fields.

more.title: SpaceX's Starship returns from orbit and is captured by launch pad arms in a dramatic first
more.summary: SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

more.title: When the Saudi desert was green: A 125,000-year-old lakeside reveals how early humans lived
more.summary: Megafauna remains, stone tools and rare plant material recovered from the 125,000-year-old lakeside site of Uruq al-Julaybah in Mundafan, southern Saudi Arabia, provide one of the most detailed pictures yet of prehistoric human life in Arabia. Together, the discoveries reveal how early people lived, hunted and used their environment during a greener, wetter period in Arabian history.

more.title: Dark matter–hunting satellite Euclid reveals record number of cosmic 'magnifying glasses'
more.summary: UBC researchers have helped uncover 15,000 new potential strong gravitational lenses—the largest collection of these cosmic tools that help astronomers investigate dark matter.

more.title: The experiments improving our understanding of volcanic tsunamis
more.summary: Tsunamis triggered by volcanic eruptions are poorly understood because of the complex dynamics governing how falling rocks and ash interact with seawater to generate waves. As a result, it is difficult to anticipate whether a volcanic flow will trigger a tsunami and, if so, how big it will be.

more.title: Tangled quantum whirlpools caught unraveling in an ultracold gas
more.summary: When a cloud of atoms is cooled close to absolute zero, its atoms can merge into a Bose–Einstein condensate (BEC): an exotic fluid in which atoms across the whole cloud share a single quantum state. Current theories predict that as a disordered quantum gas settles into this ordered state, a tangle of tiny vortices should form and gradually unravel.
